presentingComplaint: Sudden-onset, severe 'worst headache of my life' that reached maximal intensity within seconds, followed by one episode of vomiting and brief loss of consciousness.
history: A 48-year-old woman was cooking when she developed an explosive, thunderclap headache that peaked in intensity within less than a minute, described as 10/10 and unlike any headache she has had before. It was accompanied by neck stiffness, photophobia, and a single episode of vomiting. Bystanders report she briefly lost consciousness for under a minute and then appeared confused for several minutes before returning to baseline mentation. No fever, no preceding head trauma, no recent infection. She has a background of hypertension, treated inconsistently, and is a current smoker (15 pack-years). No history of anticoagulant use. No family history of known aneurysmal disease reported, though she recalls a maternal aunt who died suddenly of a 'brain bleed' at a young age.
examination: Alert but drowsy and photophobic, grimacing in a darkened room. GCS 14/15 (E4V4M6). Neck stiffness present with positive Kernig's sign. No focal motor deficit. Pupils equal and reactive; mild right partial ptosis with the right pupil slightly larger and sluggish, raising concern for a partial third-nerve palsy. Fundoscopy shows subhyaloid (pre-retinal) haemorrhages bilaterally. No papilledema noted acutely. Cardiovascular and respiratory exam unremarkable aside from elevated blood pressure.
imaging: Non-contrast CT head (within 6 hours of onset): diffuse subarachnoid blood in the basal cisterns, sylvian fissures, and interhemispheric fissure, modified Fisher grade 3
CT angiography head/neck: 6 mm saccular aneurysm at the right posterior communicating artery origin, consistent with the partial third-nerve palsy
ECG: diffuse T-wave inversions / QTc prolongation consistent with neurogenic stunned myocardium, no acute ischemic pattern
finalDiagnosis: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (right posterior communicating artery aneurysm) presenting as thunderclap headache
citations: AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage 2023
contraindications: Avoid lumbar puncture before neuroimaging in a patient with thunderclap headache and suspected raised intracranial pressure or a mass lesion
Avoid anticoagulants/antiplatelets until the aneurysm is secured

Avoid aggressive antihypertensive lowering that drops cerebral perfusion pressure before the aneurysm is secured; blood pressure should be controlled to a target (e.g. SBP <160 mmHg) rather than normalized abruptly
Nimodipine should not be given intravenously (oral/enteral only) due to hypotension risk
edgeCases: If initial CT head is done beyond 6 hours from headache onset and is negative, lumbar puncture with xanthochromia assessment is required to exclude SAH before the diagnosis can be excluded
A sentinel headache (warning leak) may precede the major bleed by days to weeks and can be misdiagnosed as migraine or tension headache
Third-nerve palsy with a dilated pupil in the context of thunderclap headache should be treated as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise
Perimesencephalic (non-aneurysmal) SAH has a similar presentation but a benign course and negative angiogram; not distinguishable from aneurysmal SAH on symptoms alone, requires imaging
expectedMaiK: Thunderclap headache with meningism, brief LOC, and a partial CN III palsy is aneurysmal SAH until proven otherwise; recommend emergent non-contrast CT head, and if negative beyond 6 hours, LP for xanthochromia, followed by CT/MR angiography to localize the aneurysm and urgent neurosurgical/neurointerventional referral for securing the aneurysm plus nimodipine for vasospasm prophylaxis.
expectedNextQuestions: Exact time of headache onset and time since symptom onset (affects CT sensitivity and LP timing)
Any preceding sentinel headache in the prior days to weeks?
Family history of aneurysm, polycystic kidney disease, or connective tissue disorder?
Any recent trauma to suggest traumatic rather than spontaneous SAH?
expectedInvestigations: CT angiography head/neck (or digital subtraction angiography)
Lumbar puncture with xanthochromia if CT negative and clinical suspicion remains

investigations: Lumbar puncture with xanthochromia if CT negative

regressionAssertions: differential includes intracerebral haemorrhage and/or meningitis as reasonable mimics
recommended investigations include non-contrast CT head as first-line study
system flags avoidance of lumbar puncture before neuroimaging and avoidance of anticoagulation pending aneurysm securing
